title: HoloPart: Completing Occluded 3D Parts with Diffusion
one_liner: HoloPart uses diffusion models to infer hidden, occluded parts of 3D objects by imagining the positions and shapes of the hidden surfaces.
lead: When you look at a 3D object from one angle, you see only the surfaces facing you. The back, the underside, the parts hidden inside the chair leg or tucked into the fold—all are invisible. For designing or editing objects, you need to know the complete shape. HoloPart imagines those hidden parts by learning patterns from thousands of 3D shapes, much like how you can imagine what a person looks like from the back even if you only see their front.

paras: Today's 3D part segmentation breaks objects into pieces—a chair becomes seat, legs, back, armrests. But it can only identify the parts it sees. If the leg is pressed against a wall, if two parts occlude each other, if the inside of a hollow object is invisible, the algorithm gives up. It marks these regions as unknown.

A beginner's first try: just ignore the occluded parts, segment only what is visible, and call it done. That fails for any real task. A designer cannot edit the hidden shape; an animation system cannot move an occluded part; a physics engine cannot reason about contact forces on surfaces you cannot see. You are flying blind.

callout.html: HoloPart learns to imagine complete 3D parts by training on full shapes, then uses its learned patterns to fill in the hidden regions.

steps.text: A 3D object with some parts visible, some occluded by other parts or the camera angle.
Existing segmentation methods label the visible parts. Occluded regions remain unknown.
The incomplete part segments, represented as 3D point clouds and surfaces, become the starting point for generation.
HoloPart applies local attention (for fine detail) and global attention (for shape fit), imagining plausible hidden surfaces that fit the object's overall structure.
All parts are now labeled and complete, including the occluded regions, ready for downstream tasks.

paras: HoloPart does not change how you segment. It does not modify the input object. Instead, it changes the initial segment map by filling in the parts that were marked unknown or occluded.

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: shape-aware completion confidence
hidden.name: Geometric plausibility score
paras: HoloPart learns to measure plausibility—how likely a completed part looks given the visible parts around it. It does not have a named score in the paper, but it implicitly learns to rate completions by how well they fit the object's overall shape consistency.

The model estimates this by comparing generated shapes to patterns learned from thousands of complete 3D objects. Shapes that match those learned patterns score high; shapes that clash or break symmetry score low. This invisible judgment guide steers diffusion toward realistic completions.

heat.caption: Darker means the diffusion model rated that geometric feature as more plausible and likely to be kept.

reads.html: The model learns which completed shapes look natural by studying many complete 3D objects. It remembers patterns like 'chair legs are roughly symmetric' and 'table undersides are flat.' When imagining an occluded part, it rates candidates by how closely they match these learned patterns.

HoloPart uses local and global attention mechanisms. Local attention scores fine geometric details (edges, curves) of the parts being completed. Global shape context attention scores how well the completed part fits the overall 3D structure. Together, these attentions implicitly measure how plausible each denoising step is.

paras: The core insight is that 3D objects follow patterns. Chairs have legs below the seat. Tables have undersides parallel to their tops. Symmetry, contact, and gravity shape real shapes. A diffusion model trained on thousands of complete objects learns these patterns deeply.

When you give HoloPart an incomplete part segment, you are handing it a puzzle: 'Here is what I see. What does the hidden part look like?' The model starts with a rough guess (noise). Then, guided by local attention (which learns edge and surface details) and global attention (which learns how parts relate to the whole object), it refines that guess step by step. At each step, it asks: Does this look plausible? Does it match learned patterns? Does it fit the visible parts? Shapes that fail these checks are pushed away; shapes that pass are kept and refined. After many steps, an invisible part crystallizes into existence—one that matches the object's learned style and constraints.

stages.s: Partial 3D shape with some parts marked unknown
Local attention: refine edges and geometric details of each part
Global attention: ensure all parts fit together and maintain overall shape
Complete 3D parts, including all formerly occluded regions

math.words: loss equals the distance between the true complete shape and the model's predicted shape, measured across both visible and occluded regions, weighted by a local attention mask and a global consistency term
math.equation: L = E[ ||x_complete - x_predicted||^2 ] + lambda_local * A_local + lambda_global * C_shape
symbols: the true full 3D shape (geometry of all parts, visible and hidden)
the geometry the diffusion model generated in this denoising step
squared distance (how far apart two geometries are)
local attention mask (higher weight on edges and fine details)
global shape consistency (penalty if parts do not align or symmetry is broken)
tuning knobs controlling how much to enforce detail vs. overall consistency

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose the model is trying to complete a chair leg.
True shape x_complete: leg has 4 vertices, height 40 units, radius 2 units.
Model's guess x_predicted: leg has height 42 units (2 too tall), radius 2 units.
Local attention mask A_local: edge of leg is important, so weight = 3. Penalty A_local = 3.
Global shape consistency C_shape: leg height slightly off but not breaking symmetry, so penalty = 0.5.
The model sees this penalty and nudges the predicted leg height down toward 40, reducing loss on the next iteration.

math.note: Each shape mismatch is scored twice: once for local fine details and once for global shape fit. Large, obvious errors (like a leg that is way too tall) are caught by C_shape; subtle edge misalignments are caught by A_local.

charts.note: Without reasoning about occlusion, you cannot complete hidden shape at all.

charts.title: HoloPart with local and global attention
charts.note: HoloPart completes hidden parts while preserving visible shape and maintaining overall shape consistency.

items.html: If a training set lacks examples of a particular shape (say, a twisted artistic sculpture), HoloPart may default to generic shape instead of capturing the true occluded form, because the pattern it learned does not cover this case.

If most of a part is hidden and very few visual cues remain, the model has little to anchor on. It may hallucinate a plausible-looking part that does not match the true shape, especially if multiple completions are equally consistent with the visible evidence.
If local attention weights fine shape too heavily, it may over-smooth or over-sharpen edges, especially near occlusion boundaries where ground truth shape transitions abruptly.

When the object is a common shape (chair, table, car) with typical occlusions (legs behind other legs, underside against floor), HoloPart excels because the training data includes these patterns, and local and global attention work together to ensure both fine detail and overall coherence.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a simple test on a single chair or table: hand-occlude (hide) one leg or the underside by masking it out. Run HoloPart's segmentation on the occluded version. Measure how well it reconstructs the true hidden shape by comparing the completed part's shape to the ground truth.
demo.metric_eq: completion_accuracy = sum of vertex distance errors for occluded parts / total occluded vertices below threshold
demo.closing: The demo should make it impossible to miss that HoloPart generates a realistic leg or underside that closely matches the original, not a featureless blob or a nonsensical bulge.
